title: Hello, what's your name?
title_target: Dia duit! Cén t-ainm atá ort?
goal: Greeting people and answering a greeting, saying your name and where you're from, asking how someone is, and meeting the two different verbs for "to be".
bekal: greet people with *Dia duit* and answer correctly
say your name with *Is mise …* and *… is ainm dom*
use *tá mé / tá tú / tá sé* to say how someone is

notes: **Dia duit literally means "God to you".** It's an everyday greeting, as neutral as "hello", used by believers and non-believers alike. The reply isn't a repeat but an addition: *Dia is Muire duit* — "God and Mary to you". If a third person greets after that, they add again: *Dia is Muire duit is Pádraig*. To more than one person: *Dia daoibh*.

**A Bhudi — calling someone changes the first letter of their name.** To address someone, Irish puts a little word *a* before the name, and that *a* brings séimhiú (lenition): *Budi* → *a Bhudi*, *Máire* → *a Mháire*, *Seán* → *a Sheáin*. The *a* itself is barely heard. It's the last trace of the old "calling" form (the vocative) that once existed across European languages, and Irish still uses it every day.

**Two ways to give your name, two different word orders.** *Is mise Budi* means "I am Budi" — right for introducing yourself. *Budi is ainm dom* is literally "Budi is a name to me", the standard answer to *Cén t-ainm atá ort?* — which itself literally means "what name is on you?". Irish puts a name **on** a person rather than giving it to them.

**Tá mé, not is mé.** Irish has two verbs for "to be". *Tá* is for states that can change — *Tá mé go maith* (I'm well), *Tá an tae réidh* (the tea's ready). *Is* is for identity — *Is mise Máire*, *Is as an Indinéis mé*. Mixing them up is the most common beginner mistake, and Unit 13 is devoted to it.

blocks.text: *Níl a fhios agam* literally means "its knowledge is not at me" — notice *fhios*, whose f is completely silent, so it sounds like "IS". A short form just as common in speech: *N'fheadar* (NYAH-dar) in Munster.

blocks.title: One sentence that changes your experience of Ireland
items: *Tá mé ag foghlaim Gaeilge. An bhfuil Gaeilge agat?* — "I'm learning Irish. Do you speak Irish?"

Every Irish speaker is also fluent in English, so they switch automatically the moment they hear a foreign accent. The sentence above stops the switch — and it's almost always met with a smile, because outsiders who learn their language are still rare.
Notice how it's built: Irish doesn't say "you speak Irish" but "is there Irish **at** you". Even an ability is treated as something you have. Unit 7 covers this in full.

sections.title: Greetings for every time and situation

blocks.text: Irish doesn't split greetings by the clock the way English does with "good morning" and "good evening". *Dia duit* works all day. What changes with the time of day is the **goodbye** and the night-time blessing.

blocks.title: Three ways to answer "Conas atá tú?"
items: *Tá mé go maith* (taw may guh MAH) — well. The neutral answer that's always safe.
*Tá mé go breá* (taw may guh BRAW) — great. A little warmer.
*Níl mé go maith* (neel may guh MAH) — I'm not well. Notice that *níl* replaces the whole of *tá*; it doesn't add a "not" in front.
The word *go* before an adjective turns it into an adverb, like English "-ly". If the adjective begins with a vowel, *go* adds an h: *go hiontach*, *go hálainn*.

blocks.text: The "how are you" question itself varies by region, and all three are correct: *Conas atá tú?* (the south and the standard), *Cén chaoi a bhfuil tú?* (kyayn KHEE uh WIL too — Galway and Connacht), *Cad é mar atá tú?* (kod ay mar uh-TAW too — Donegal and Ulster). This course uses the first because it's shortest, but don't be surprised to hear the other two.

*Tá* means "is/am/are" or "there is", and it's the most used verb in Irish. Notice two things at once: it stands **before** the subject, and it **doesn't change** for different people — only the pronoun changes.

For "I" and "we" there are short fused forms: *táim* (TAW-im) and *táimid* (TAW-mid). They're just as correct as *tá mé* and *tá muid*, and more common in the south. This course uses the separate forms because their structure is easier to see.

blocks.title: Trap: the verb sits up front
items: English says "Máire is happy"; Irish says "is Máire happy" — *Tá Máire sásta*. The verb is **always** the first word in a statement.
So never start a sentence with a name or a pronoun. *Mé tá go maith* is wrong; the right form is *Tá mé go maith*.
This order is called verb–subject–object, and Irish shares it with Arabic, Welsh and Tagalog — not with English.
